questions.scenario: Every accepted checkout change produces a validated, deployable package. Production waits for an authorized release decision, but the deployment procedure itself is automated. Which description best matches this setup?

options.text: It is continuous deployment because creating a package is a production release.
It is neither delivery nor deployment because a human decision remains.
It is continuous delivery with a deliberate production approval gate.
It is only continuous integration because deployment automation cannot have gates.

questions.explanation: A release-ready, validated package with an automated path can support continuous delivery while retaining a human production decision. That decision distinguishes it from automatically deploying every accepted change; packaging alone is not deployment. [Official reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments).

questions.scenario: Staging verified digest A from commit abc123. Production rebuilt commit abc123 and deployed digest B. The release log cites staging's result as proof that production's package passed verification. What does the evidence establish?

options.text: Only A was verified; production needs the tested artifact or independent validation of B.
A and B are interchangeable because a commit identifies every build input.
The later build inherits staging's verification because it ran afterward.
Matching package names are sufficient even when their contents differ.

questions.explanation: Commit identity is not byte identity. Build inputs and processes may differ, and the digest mismatch identifies different artifacts. Sequence and names do not transfer verification evidence between them. [Official reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/use-artifact-attestations).

questions.scenario: An authorized reviewer approves the release, but staging smoke verification fails against the candidate package. The team configured both approval and successful verification as requirements. What should happen?

options.text: Proceed because approval implicitly overrides technical checks.
Rebuild in production and retain the approval without further verification.
Treat the failed check as informational once the package was approved.
Keep production blocked until the required verification succeeds for the candidate.

questions.explanation: Approval and technical verification address different requirements. Neither automatically cancels the other. Rebuilding also changes the candidate; continuing or downgrading the check violates the stated release contract. [Official reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments).

questions.scenario: A release removed a database field that the previous application version requires. The new version then starts returning errors. An operator proposes deploying the old binary immediately. What is the safest first decision?

options.text: Roll back the binary because version order proves database compatibility.
Assess current data compatibility and choose a compatible recovery or roll-forward path.
Rebuild the old binary so it automatically learns the changed database schema.
Ignore the database change because the application image is immutable.

questions.explanation: Recovery must account for persistent state already changed, not just a previous binary. Rebuilding or image immutability does not restore a removed field. The scenario requires a compatible recovery path before changing traffic or software again. [Official reference](https://sre.google/sre-book/release-engineering/).

questions.scenario: A candidate has low CPU usage and a passed staging check. Production serves much higher traffic and uses different external dependencies. Which two checks strengthen the decision to continue a gradual release?

options.text: Verify the deployed candidate's digest matches the package whose evidence was reviewed.
Assume staging success proves production dependency behavior at all traffic levels.
Compare candidate behavior with a stable baseline over a meaningful observation window.
Promote as soon as the process starts, before customer requests reach it.

questions.explanation: Artifact identity connects evidence to the candidate, while observed behavior tests its production impact. Low CPU, startup, or staging success alone cannot cover different production conditions. [Official reference](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/).
